topic.label: EEG & Signal Methods
topic.description: EEG signal processing, sleep staging, neural time series, modeling, and practical analysis methods.

papers.title: Protocol-aware dual-view single-channel EEG sleep staging with improved N1 discrimination on public sleep-EDF and SHHS benchmarks.
papers.abstract: To develop and evaluate DualViewSeqSleepNet, a protocol-aware single-channel EEG model for automatic sleep staging under reproducible public benchmark settings. The model integrates raw-waveform and spectral encoders, gated epoch-level fusion, lightweight bidirectional cross-epoch aggregation, and an auxiliary loss targeting Wake-N1 and N1-N2 transitions. Primary testing used the exact Sleep-EDF SC-subset protocol of SeriesSleepNet. Secondary no-retuning evaluation used SHHS-1 healthy C4-A1 data. On Sleep-EDF, DualViewSeqSleepNet achieved macro-F1 0.821, accuracy 0.869, and Cohen's kappa 0.808, exceeding the SeriesSleepNet anchor and improving N1 F1 from 0.506 to 0.535. On SHHS-1, it reached macro-F1 0.791 and accuracy 0.854 without architecture-family retuning. Ablation and robustness analyses supported the contributions of dual-view fusion, cross-epoch aggregation, and N1-aware supervision. DualViewSeqSleepNet provides a modest, protocol-aligned improvement for public single-channel sleep staging, especially near Wake-N1-N2 boundaries, but does not establish external clinical validation or autonomous deployment readiness.

papers.title: MLE EEG Toolbox: A Personal AI Laboratory Assistant for Literature-Informed and Reproducible M/EEG Research
papers.abstract: Electrophysiological research increasingly relies on complex analytical workflows, yet integrating methodological evidence, computational execution and reproducibility remains challenging. Here we introduce MLE EEG Toolbox, a framework for building a personal AI laboratory assistant for electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) research. The toolbox integrates locally deployed AI, natural-language-guided analysis, literature retrieval and methodological comparison, and reproducible computational workflows. A constrained language model translates research instructions into validated, researcher-approved operations, while literature-informed guidance supports parameter selection and protocol reconstruction. Computational provenance enables transparent inspection and replay of analytical workflows. The assistant achieved action-selection accuracies of 85.6% for EEG and 95.5% for MEG, while 142 cross-platform tests demonstrated close numerical agreement. Applications to public EEG and MEG datasets illustrated integrated spectral, network, decoding and source analyses. Running on standard personal computers without external AI APIs or token charges, MLE EEG Toolbox provides an accessible, researcher-controlled environment that connects methodological knowledge with reproducible electrophysiological analysis.

papers.title: From clusters to curves: A model-based alternative to cluster-based permutation tests for the analysis of time-resolved data
papers.abstract: Time-resolved electrophysiological measurements such as those obtained through magneto- and electroencephalography (M/EEG) offer a unique window onto the neural activity underlying cognitive processes. Researchers are often interested in determining whether and when these signals differ across experimental conditions or participant groups. The conventional approach involves mass univariate statistical testing across time and space followed by corrections for multiple comparisons or some form of cluster-based inference. While effective for controlling error rates at the cluster-level, cluster-based inference comes with a significant limitation: by shifting the focus of inference from individual time points to clusters, it prevents drawing conclusions about the precise onset or offset of observed effects. Here, we present a model-based alternative for analysing M/EEG time series, such as event-related potentials or time-resolved decoding accuracy. Our approach leverages Bayesian generalised additive multilevel models, providing posterior odds at each time point, while naturally accounting for between-participant variability. Using simulated data with known ground truth, we show that the proposed approach consistently provides accurate recovery of the overall temporal extent and onset of neural effects across a range of signal-to-noise ratios, although offset localisation is comparatively more variable. In an empirical MEG decoding dataset, the approach also yields the highest split-half temporal overlap among the methods considered and highly stable temporal segmentation across repeated participant splits. Together, these results illustrate the potential of model-based inference as a complementary approach to conventional cluster-based procedures when temporally localised inference and explicit modelling of between-participant variability are scientifically important. We provide an open-source R package implementing the method and describe how it can be integrated into M/EEG analysis pipelines using MNE-Python.

ai.summary: Proposed a model-based alternative to cluster-based permutation testing for M/EEG time-resolved data using Bayesian generalized additive multilevel models that yield posterior odds at each time point while accounting for between-participant variability. Simulations recovered effect onset and extent accurately across signal-to-noise ratios, and an empirical MEG decoding dataset showed the highest split-half temporal overlap among compared methods.

papers.title: Hidden Drowsiness in Wakefulness: Differences in Resting-State EEG Profiles in Natural Short Sleepers Versus Recommended Length Sleepers.
papers.abstract: Chronic insufficient sleep affects cardiovascular, endocrine, immune and nervous systems and is linked to cognitive decline and increased mortality. Among habitual short sleepers, a subgroup known as natural short sleepers (NSS) report sleeping ≤ 6 h per night without experiencing subjective daytime dysfunction. However, discrepancies between subjective and objective markers of alertness raise questions about their true cognitive state. NSS have been described as high in behavioural activation, a phenotype overlapping with ADHD and mania in which dysregulation of resting-state brain arousal has been well documented. Despite these parallels, few studies have investigated the neurophysiological features of NSS. The current study examined resting-state EEG in NSS and recommended-length sleepers (RLS) during eyes-open conditions. Results showed that NSS exhibited significantly higher global alpha power and regionally steeper aperiodic exponents, particularly in occipital areas, both markers of increased drowsiness. Although global exponent values did not differ significantly, a significant Group × Region interaction was observed and NSS showed a trend toward increasing aperiodic exponents over time, suggesting less stable wakefulness under low-stimulation conditions. These findings point to subtle neurophysiological differences in NSS, raising the possibility that their perceived resilience to short sleep may mask underlying drowsiness.

papers.title: Directional brain-heart interaction during cognitive workload: a permutation conditional mutual information approach.
papers.abstract: The functional interaction between the central nervous system and autonomic cardiovascular regulation, commonly referred to as Brain-Heart Interaction (BHI), has gained increasing attention in neurology and psychology through the joint analysis of Electroencephalography (EEG) and Electrocardiography (ECG) signals. However, the nonlinear and time-varying nature of EEG and ECG signals requires approaches that can capture directional interactions between physiological systems. In this study, we investigated the use of Permutation Conditional Mutual Information (PCMI) for the characterization of directional BHI. First, the method was evaluated on synthetically generated coupled time series to assess its ability to detect the dominant direction of interaction. Next, PCMI was applied to simultaneous EEG and ECG recordings acquired during baseline and mental arithmetic tasks from a cohort of 36 subjects. The results show that BHI complexity increases during mental arithmetic tasks compared with baseline, supporting the role of cognitive workload in modulating brain-heart dynamics. These changes primarily involved anterior and posterior scalp regions, and affected both vagal- and sympathovagal-related HRV components. These findings demonstrate that PCMI provides a framework for studying directional BHI during cognitive tasks, and highlight its potential translational value for investigating broader brain-body interactions.

Brain-heart interaction complexity increased during mental arithmetic, mainly involving anterior and posterior scalp regions and vagal- and sympathovagal-related HRV components.

papers.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
papers.abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

ai.reason: Provides controllable synthetic EEG for training and benchmarking lightweight models, useful for data augmentation and algorithm development, though disorder-focused rather than sleep-oriented.
ai.summary: Presents NeuroSim, an open-source framework generating synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific spectral patterns across five disorders and severity levels, reproducing expected biomarkers. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3–96.8% hold-out accuracy, and augmenting real clinical EEG with NeuroSim samples improved AD vs. control accuracy from 91.6% to 94.5% and PD vs. control from 90.9% to 94.0%.

papers.title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control. Much of what we know about brain function comes from measuring how neural activity responds to specific events, from sensory stimuli and cognitive demands to targeted pulses of brain stimulation. Tracking these responses is fundamental for mapping how brain networks communicate in health and disease and for guiding interventions that modulate neural circuits. Because each response is buried in ongoing background activity and changes across repetitions, isolating it is difficult. Existing methods average repetitions inside short, hand-picked time windows, restricting researchers to seeing only the earliest, most stereotyped part of a response while leaving later, fluctuating activity invisible. Here, we introduce a new approach that combines the pattern-finding sensitivity of modern machine learning with the strict false-positive control of traditional statistics. Our method searches the period after each event without a preset window, using recordings of the brain at rest both to learn how a response differs from normal background activity and to measure what the model detects by chance alone. Using this tool, we show that human brain responses to electrical stimulation last over twice as long as previously recognized, revealing that brief perturbations trigger a longer cascade of neural activity than previously thought.

papers.title: Seizure Prediction Using Channel-Optimized Intracranial EEG With Variable Interictal and Preictal Durations.
papers.abstract: Objective: Predicting epileptic seizures using electroencephalogram (EEG) signals can provide a critical window for intervention to suppress impending seizures. However, the impact of varying interictal and preictal durations on seizure prediction remains unclear and warrants further exploration. Considering this, this study focuses on seizure prediction using intracranial EEG (iEEG) signals with variable interictal and preictal durations. Method: In this work, we discuss six pairwise combinations in total, involving two interictal durations (24 h and 48 h) and three preictal durations (30 min, 60 min and 90 min), during seizure prediction analysis. Furthermore, we also compare three classification strategies: the all-channel strategy (Strategy 1), the single-channel-based majority voting strategy (Strategy 2) and the channel-optimization-based majority voting strategy (Strategy 3), across each pairwise combination. Results: The long-term SWEC-ETHZ iEEG dataset is utilized to evaluate our method. The results reveal that our method achieves up to 87.7 sensitivity, 94.6 specificity, 92.8 accuracy, 0.912 Area Under the Curve (AUC) and 0.858 F1-score at the segment-based level, along with 95.9 sensitivity and 0.05/h false prediction rate (FPR) at the event-based level. Moreover, the overall performance of Strategy 3 surpasses that of Strategies 1 and 2 in each pairwise combination, indicating that channel optimization is beneficial for improving seizure prediction performance. Conclusion: This work shows high effectiveness in predicting seizures using iEEG signals, with the ability to forecast upcoming epileptic events up to 90 min in advance across both 24-h and 48-h interictal durations.

Channel optimization performed best in every combination, reaching up to 87.7% sensitivity, 94.6% specificity, 0.912 AUC at the segment level and 95.9% sensitivity with 0.05/h FPR at the event level, forecasting seizures up to 90 min ahead.

papers.title: A shared slowing axis and phenotype-specific rhythms link clinical EEG to FDG-PET dementia phenotypes.
papers.abstract: Early and accurate identification of neurodegenerative disorders has notable implications for treatment and quality of life. Whereas neuroimaging-based biomarkers can accurately identify neurodegenerative subtypes, EEG represents a low-cost alternative that could expand access to dementia care. Here, we investigated whether six data-driven EEG latent factors, derived by nonnegative tensor decomposition of clinical EEGs, differ systematically across FDG-PET-defined neurodegenerative phenotypes. In 455 patients with EEG and FDG-PET acquired within one year of each other, factor expression was compared across 14 diagnostic classes assigned by StateViewer, a validated artificial intelligence framework for FDG-PET interpretation. To separate disease-general severity from phenotype-specific topography, each factor was also regressed on a subject-level slowing index. Finally, we related the factors to regional FDG uptake and to neuropsychological performance (n = 98) and assessed their potential utility for single-subject classification. Four factors reflecting neurophysiological oscillations (posterior alpha, Rolandic beta, frontotemporal delta-theta and posterior theta-slow alpha) varied significantly across phenotypes, with attenuation of faster and augmentation of slower rhythms most pronounced in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), dysexecutive Alzheimer disease (AD) and posterior cortical atrophy, whereas factors dominated by eye-movement and muscle artifact showed no robust phenotypic association. Alpha and beta effects were largely attributable to overall slowing, whereas posterior theta-slow alpha became more phenotype-specific after adjustment (eta-squared 0.082 to 0.147), dissociating the Alzheimer disease spectrum from frontotemporal syndromes. The slowing index tracked with an FDG-PET pattern highly associated with DLB across the cohort, irrespective of assigned phenotype (r = 0.51, P < 0.001). Consistent with a model in which dementia phenotypes reflect altered hippocampal-neocortical oscillatory coupling (stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion), frontotemporal delta-theta tracked a limbocortical axis of metabolic pattern expression, rising with neocortical and falling with limbic-predominant involvement, independent of overall slowing and phenotype. Each factor mapped onto a distinct metabolic topography, with frontotemporal delta-theta resembling Alzheimer-type hypometabolism and posterior theta-slow alpha the medial occipital hypometabolism of DLB. In terms of neuropsychological performance, Rolandic beta was associated with executive functions, and frontotemporal delta-theta with memory, visuospatial and global performance. Using these four factors alone, an exploratory logistic regression classifier separated cognitively unimpaired participants from DLB, posterior cortical atrophy, typical AD, and dysexecutive AD (area under the curve > 0.8) but poorly discriminated frontotemporal dementia phenotypes canonically associated with 4-repeat tau. Thus, data-driven decomposition of clinical EEG separates oscillatory activity from artifact into factors that track metabolic phenotype, regional metabolism and cognition, capturing both overall slowing and phenotype-specific patterns. This work informs the further development of scalable, biology-informed EEG-based phenotyping of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: FUSE: FUsing EEG-MEG in a Shared Embedding via self-supervised learning for BCI
papers.abstract: Combining complementary neurophysiological modalities offers a promising strategy for improving motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), but learning shared representations across modalities remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a two-phase deep learning framework for multimodal EEG-MEG decoding that explicitly decouples representation learning from downstream classification. In the first phase, a convolutional encoder-decoder learns a shared latent representation by predicting the power spectral density (PSD) of EEG and MEG signals directly from time-domain activity, rather than using the conventional objective of reconstructing the input signal. In the second phase, the encoder is frozen and its learned representations are reused, without further adaptation, to perform the classification of the downstream MI-BCI task. The framework was evaluated on simultaneous EEG and MEG recordings from 20 participants. The learned representations consistently outperformed conventional handcrafted spectral features, increasing median classification accuracy from 0.734 to 0.794. The multimodal framework also improved performance over MEG alone (median accuracy from 0.680 to 0.794) and yielded a modest increase over EEG alone (median accuracy from 0.765 to 0.794), providing a more robust decoding strategy than single-modality approaches. Furthermore, the learned latent representations were transferable across participants, with more than half of cross-subject models performing within 0.01 accuracy of their subject-specific counterparts. These findings demonstrate that task-agnostic representation learning can capture physiologically meaningful multimodal neural representations that remain transferable across individuals, offering a promising foundation for more robust and reusable BCI pipelines.

ai.summary: Introduces FUSE, a two-phase self-supervised framework that learns a shared EEG-MEG latent representation by predicting power spectral density from time-domain activity and then reuses the frozen encoder for motor imagery BCI classification. On simultaneous EEG-MEG from 20 participants, the learned representations raised median accuracy from 0.734 with handcrafted spectral features to 0.794, also outperforming MEG alone (0.680) and slightly EEG alone (0.765), with cross-subject transfer within 0.01 accuracy for over half of models.

papers.title: The Potency Stability Tradeoff: Evaluating EEG Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder.
papers.abstract: BackgroundIdentifying objective EEG biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) remains a challenge due to poor model robustness and a lack of clarity regarding which neural parameters are sufficiently stable for clinical translation.ObjectiveThis study deconstructs the MDD neuro-signature to evaluate the critical tradeoff between predictive power and biomarker stability.MethodsUsing EEG data from 30 MDD patients and 88 controls, we constructed a high-dimensional feature space comprising connectivity, spectral, and complexity measures. The investigation was multi-stage and a leakage-free cross-validation framework. The feature space was decomposed by modality and frequency band using a non-linear XGBoost pipeline to determine the best sources of predictive information. We compared a model utilizing fold-specific top features against one based on stable biomarkers discovered via a strictly nested, leakage-free Stability-Optimized Consensus Learning (SOCL) framework.FindingsThe strongest predictive signals were localized to Theta (4-8 Hz) and Alpha (8-13 Hz) bands (max AUC = 0.683). However, these spectral features were highly inconsistent across data subsets (mean Jaccard Index = 0.187), resulting in substantial overfitting. In contrast, the model trained on stable biomarkers, selected by a leakage-free consensus of linear and non-linear feature selection, achieved superior generalization performance (AUC = 0.792 vs 0.662) and showed significantly less overfitting (P<.05 via permutation test).ConclusionThe MDD neuro-signature exists in two forms: a potent but unstable signal associated with Theta-Alpha dysregulation and a weaker but highly stable signal embedded within the functional connectome. These findings suggest that biomarker stability is more important than signal strength for developing clinically reliable diagnostic tools.

ai.reason: Leakage-free nested cross-validation and stability-optimized feature selection are relevant methodological practices for reproducible EEG pipelines, but the study is a specific MDD biomarker application.
ai.summary: Deconstructed EEG-based MDD biomarkers using connectivity, spectral, and complexity features from 30 MDD patients and 88 controls under leakage-free cross-validation, finding Theta-Alpha signals maximally predictive (AUC 0.683) but unstable (Jaccard 0.187), while stability-optimized consensus feature selection gave superior generalization (AUC 0.792 vs 0.662). Concludes biomarker stability matters more than signal strength for clinically reliable diagnostics.

papers.title: Intrarater reliability of expert electroencephalographic interpretation of 100 full-length recordings.
papers.abstract: The value of electroencephalography (EEG) relies on accurate and reliable interpretation. Prior research has demonstrated imperfect interrater reliability, but intrarater reliability remains poorly characterized. We performed a "noise audit" primarily to measure intrarater variability in EEG interpretation by epileptologists. Experts independently rated the same 100 full-length EEGs on two separate occasions ≥60 days apart, unaware the EEGs were the same. EEGs were recorded from adult (56%) and pediatric patients in outpatient (78%) and non-critical care inpatient settings. There were 20 studies in each of five categories: normal, focal epileptiform (FE), generalized epileptiform (GE), focal nonepileptiform (FNE), and generalized nonepileptiform (GNE) abnormalities. EEGs were presented using our online platform (EEGHub) without clinical information except for age and sex. Experts rated each recording and indicated their level of confidence (LOC) for each EEG and overall. We analyzed percent as well as chance-corrected intra- and interrater agreement. Fourteen experts (mean of 19 years EEG reading experience, range = 4-52 years) were included in the study. Percent self-agreement was 96% for GE, 90% for FE, 88% for FNE, and 87% for GNE abnormalities; 90% for any epileptiform abnormality; and 82% for any nonepileptiform abnormality. Self-agreement was strongly correlated with interrater agreement (mean κML), which was almost perfect for GE (.90, 95% confidence interval [CI] = .87-.94) and FE (.82, 95% CI = .77-.87) and substantial for GNE (.75, 95% CI = .69-.81) and FNE (.74, 95% CI = .68-.80) abnormalities. LOC correlated with self-agreement on the presence of nonepileptiform but not epileptiform abnormalities. We found generally strong within-expert agreement in EEG interpretation, especially in the identification of epileptiform abnormalities. Nevertheless, the number of flipped decisions was high enough to be clinically consequential. This undesired variability ("occasion noise") may be addressed by interventions to (1) decrease this noise directly and (2) reduce case ambiguity with longer recordings and better EEG data whenever feasible.

ai.reason: Reliability of expert EEG interpretation touches on labeling reliability and benchmark quality, adjacent to but not directly about computational methods.
ai.summary: Conducted a 'noise audit' in which 14 expert epileptologists independently rated the same 100 full-length EEGs on two occasions at least 60 days apart to measure intrarater reliability. Percent self-agreement ranged from 96% for generalized epileptiform to 82% for any nonepileptiform abnormality, with strong correlation to interrater agreement, though flipped decisions were frequent enough to be clinically consequential.

papers.title: Frontotemporal Slow-Frequency Dominance in Quantitative EEG as a Potential Biomarker of Post-COVID Cognitive Dysfunction.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo characterize quantitative electroencephalographic alterations associated with persistent cognitive complaints following mild COVID-19 and to explore their relationship with cognitive performance and their discriminative potential.MethodsIn this exploratory case-control study, qEEG recordings from 21 patients with persistent cognitive complaints following mild COVID-19 infection and 21 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were analyzed. Subject-level spectral power and slow-to-fast frequency ratios were quantified using a harmonized 14-electrode common-average reference. Associations with Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) performance were explored within the post-COVID group using univariate Random Forest regression. Exploratory classification was performed using 112 spectral qEEG features with leakage-controlled repeated cross-validation and training-fold-specific feature selection.ResultsPost-COVID patients showed a spatially heterogeneous shift toward slower spectral activity, with the most consistent differences involving frontal electrodes and the right temporal region. Cognitive associations were modest and domain-specific, with the clearest out-of-sample performance observed for identification/naming (best mean cross-validated R2 = 0.328 ± 0.319). Leakage-controlled classification showed substantial exploratory discriminative performance between patients and controls: logistic regression achieved a weighted F1-score of 0.877 ± 0.109 (ROC-AUC = 0.947), and Random Forest achieved 0.898 ± 0.123 (ROC-AUC = 0.949).ConclusionsThese findings suggest spectral qEEG alterations in patients with persistent cognitive complaints following mild COVID-19, predominantly involving frontal and right-temporal slow-frequency activity. Cognitive and classification findings remain exploratory and require confirmation in larger independent cohorts.
authors: María Mar González Álvarez de Sotomayor

Findings require confirmation in larger independent cohorts.

papers.title: Next generation Human Neocortical Neurosolver model with biophysically realistic somatic, dendritic and synaptic dynamics.
papers.abstract: The Human Neocortical Neurosolver (HNN) is an open-source biophysical modeling tool for multiscale interpretation of human electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals. HNN's foundation is a pre-tuned canonical neocortical circuit model consisting of excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in supra- (L2/3) and infragranular (L5) layers. This model was originally developed based on studies in rodent and non-human primate cortices when dynamics of human neurons were poorly characterized. Yet recent advances in recordings from human tissue now provide unprecedented detail to update the model. Here, we present a significantly updated model for use in the HNN software, with electrophysiological properties and synaptic connections tuned to human tissue. Beyond reproducing biologically realistic somatic dynamics, the pyramidal cells simulate dendritic calcium (Ca 2+ ) spikes in the L5 extratelencephalic-projecting (ET) neurons, and shorter dendritic spikes in the L2/3 pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate how the updated circuitry and new features in the HNN software can be used to disentangle somatic, synaptic, and dendritic contributions to human E-/MEG signatures. The model is distributed with workflows to simulate event-related responses and oscillations, and tutorials demonstrating how membrane potentials, Ca 2+ dynamics, and synaptic currents can be recorded and visualized. These enhancements allow extensive model validations based on in vitro and in vivo electrophysiology, voltage and Ca 2+ imaging, and provide users with novel insights on the mechanisms underlying E-/MEG signals.

papers.title: Altered oscillatory coupling and a candidate inhibitory circuit mechanism in Rett syndrome
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused primarily by pathogenic variants in the MECP2 gene and characterized by severe cognitive and neurological impairment. Phase amplitude coupling (PAC), a cross-frequency interaction supporting information integration across temporal and spatial scales, provides a window into large-scale neural coordination and circuit dysfunction. PAC depends on coordinated activity among specific neuronal subtypes, yet the cellular mechanisms shaping oscillatory dynamics in RTT remain poorly understood. Here we combined electroencephalography (EEG) with biophysically constrained computational modeling to characterize PAC alterations and investigate their circuit-level origins. Awake resting-state EEG was recorded from 42 individuals with RTT and 37 typically developing participants, and PAC strength was quantified. Individuals with RTT exhibited stronger PAC across widespread frequency pairs and cortical regions, including elevated theta gamma coupling in posterior, midline, and whole brain regions, and elevated alpha gamma coupling in anterior, posterior, and whole brain regions. Biophysically constrained network simulations of a cortical Layer 4 model comprising pyramidal neurons together with PV+, SOM+, and VIP+ interneurons demonstrated that reduced excitability of VIP+ interneurons selectively reproduced the increased theta gamma and alpha gamma PAC observed in RTT. These findings identify abnormal PAC as an electrophysiological feature of RTT and suggest a possible mechanistic link between altered oscillatory coordination and VIP+ interneuron dysfunction. PAC may provide a non-invasive marker of inhibitory circuit dysfunction and a translational framework for investigating shared circuit abnormalities across neurodevelopmental disorders.

papers.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
papers.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

papers.title: False-Positive Calls of Reimplemented Published Analyses for Covert Command-Following on Electroencephalograms Recorded Without Study Commands.
papers.abstract: To measure how often published electroencephalographic analyses for covert command-following call patients positive without commands, and their detection of genuine responses. This cross-sectional study applied 11 reimplemented published analyses to electroencephalograms without commands: 974 clinical electroencephalography patients and, with rules fixed, 730 new patients; 38 with prolonged disorders of consciousness; and 544 comatose patients after cardiac arrest. Outcomes: false calls (share called positive) against a 5% benchmark, and genuine-response detection. Three of 10 command-following analyses called significantly more than 5% of clinical electroencephalography patients positive, replicated in new patients: Goldfine 2011, a spectral test, 23.3% (95% CI, 20.2%-26.6%), above its stated 5%; du Bois 2026, a criterion for entry to brain-computer interface training, 22.2% (95% CI, 19.2%-25.5%); and Guger 2018, a P300 accuracy threshold, 13.8% (95% CI, 11.5%-16.3%), near its approximate 12% chance rate (24.5% over 2 runs). The other 7 called 0.0% to 6.9%. After cardiac arrest: 11.5% to 27.3%. All 3 detected genuine responses. Identified contributors: a variance ignoring within-command dependence (Goldfine 2011), selection over configurations and times (du Bois 2026) and a permissive threshold (Guger 2018). Goldfine 2011's command-level correction, fixed before testing, called 0.8% of new patients and 2.4% after arrest, detecting 93.4% of stroke imagery-versus-rest sessions but few between imagery types. Reimplemented published analyses called up to 27% of patients positive without commands, more with repeated runs. A positive result needs its complete call rule's false-call rate and detection at that rate; imagery-versus-rest detection may reflect task engagement, not imagery.

papers.title: Video-Based Automated Seizure Classification Using Multimodal Large Language Models.
papers.abstract: Accurately distinguishing between epileptic seizures (ES) and nonepileptic seizures (NES) remains a significant clinical challenge, typically requiring resource-intensive inpatient video-EEG monitoring. We developed a multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based framework for automated extraction of semiological features from seizure videos, followed by classification of events as ES or NES. We analyzed 90 seizure videos (45 ES, 45 NES) from 29 patients in an epilepsy monitoring unit. Each event was labeled using expert-reviewed video-EEG and annotated for 24 clinically relevant semiological features. An MLLM framework integrating open-source vision-language models (VLMs) and audio-language models (ALMs) was used to extract these features automatically. The extracted features were then used to train classifiers (K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and Deep Factorization Machine) to distinguish ES from NES. Model performance was evaluated using leave-one-patient-out (LOPO) cross-validation. Expert-annotated features yielded near-perfect classification using KNN (precision = 0.92, recall = 0.92, F1-score = 0.92, AUC = 0.99). Compared to expert annotations, the MLLM pipeline achieved a mean recall of 0.71, accuracy of 0.58, and F1-score of 0.51 for feature extraction. Using MLLM-extracted features, the KNN classifier (k = 7) achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.76, F1-score of 0.76, and AUC of 0.76, correctly identifying 68 out of 90 events. Multimodal large language models can extract clinically relevant semiological features from seizure videos and support interpretable classification of ES versus NES. This approach offers a scalable, explainable tool to assist in video-based epilepsy diagnosis.

papers.title: Neuromodulation of cortical networks facilitates motor generalization of balance training in older adults.
papers.abstract: Motor generalization, the ability to transfer learned motor skills to untrained contexts, declines with aging and limits the functional benefits of rehabilitation. Although transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS) has been implicated in neuroplasticity, its potential to facilitate motor generalization and associated cortical network reorganization in older adults remains unclear. Forty community-dwelling older adults (69.2 ± 4.3 years) were randomly assigned to receive either tVNS (n = 20) or sham stimulation (n = 20) during stabilometer balance training. Motor generalization was assessed on the day following training using an untrained foam-stance task. Postural regulation was characterized using center-of-pressure (COP) measures, stabilogram diffusion analysis, a composite control index (CCI), and sample entropy (SampEn). Cortical network organization was examined using beta-band electroencephalography (EEG) functional connectivity and minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis. Compared with sham stimulation, tVNS-assisted training produced greater improvements in COP area, accompanied by changes in postural dynamics, CCI, and SampEn. MST analyses revealed increased leaf fraction and reduced average eccentricity and network diameter, although baseline-adjusted analyses provided the most consistent support for average eccentricity. Exploratory correlations further showed that changes in average eccentricity were associated with changes in critical displacement and CCI after false discovery rate correction. These findings suggest that tVNS-assisted balance training may enhance short-term transfer of postural learning in older adults, accompanied by cortical network topology reorganization. The observed neural-behavioral associations support the functional relevance of network changes but do not establish a causal mediating mechanism.

papers.title: Electric and Magnetic Source Imaging in Epilepsy: Anatomical Insights from Realistic Simulations.
papers.abstract: Neurosurgery is an effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), but its success depends on the accurate delineation of the epileptogenic focus, approximated noninvasively by electric and magnetic source imaging (ESI/MSI) of high-density electroencephalography (HD-EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). These modalities have distinct sensitivity profiles; consequently, epileptiform activity detected by one modality may remain undetected by the other. However, the implications of these differences for spike detectability and localization accuracy, and the added value of combined electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), remain insufficiently characterized under clinically realistic conditions. Here, we characterize HD-EEG and MEG sensitivity profiles and compare ESI, MSI, and EMSI, using realistic simulations with known ground truth. We generated HD-EEG and MEG datasets from cortical, insular, and hippocampal sources across multiple orientations, activated using patient-derived intracranial EEG spike waveforms. Spike sensitivity and localization accuracy were evaluated using dipole scanning, dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV). EEG demonstrated higher spike detection rates and sensitivity for radially cortical sources at gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms ( p <0.001), while MEG detected more spikes from tangential cortical sources along sulcal walls ( p <0.001). MSI localized tangential sources more accurately than ESI across all methods ( p <0.001), while dipole scanning outperformed dSPM and LCMV for cortical and insular sources ( p <0.001). EMSI outperformed ESI ( p <0.001) but did not improve localization over MSI. These findings suggest that complementary anatomical sensitivities of HD-EEG and MEG may improve epileptogenic source characterization, supporting simultaneous acquisition during the presurgical evaluation of patients with DRE. EEG and MEG exhibit complementary sensitivity profiles, with EEG detecting more spikes from gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms and MEG from sulcal walls.MSI provides more focal and precise source localization than ESI, particularly for tangentially oriented sources.Dipole-based inverse method achieves higher localization accuracy than experimental dSPM and LCMV.

papers.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,Ω$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

papers.title: Temporal dissociation across the eye-brain-muscle cascade delineates a preparation window before muscle activation in subacute stroke.
papers.abstract: Upper-limb motor impairment after stroke is compounded by a disrupted sensorimotor cascade linking visual attention, cortical motor preparation, and peripheral muscle activation. Whether these stages are temporally dissociated in subacute stroke, and whether their timing carries information about the preparation and execution of a reaching action, remains unclear. Thirty subacute stroke survivors and 30 healthy controls performed a full-plane nine-grid reaching task while eye-tracking, electroencephalography (EEG), and surface electromyography (EMG) were recorded synchronously. Three neurophysiological latencies were extracted: first fixation on the target, stimulus-locked lateralized readiness potential (s-LRP) onset, and peripheral muscle activation onset. Compared with controls, patients showed a stepwise delay across the cascade, with delayed visual engagement (616.73 ms vs. 367.86 ms) and delayed peripheral muscle activation (1,080 ms vs. 605 ms) bracketing a cortical preparation window. A random-forest classifier was trained on window-level gaze-timing features, computed separately for each target-presentation and inter-target interval of the task. Under participant-level leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, it achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.973 (95% CI 0.958-0.984) and an accuracy of 0.918, numerically the highest among the five classifiers compared. These findings describe a quantifiable temporal organization of the sensorimotor cascade in the subacute stage of stroke and indicate that gaze timing carries discriminative information about the occurrence of an instructed reaching action. They establish a descriptive, testable framework rather than a demonstrated clinical benefit. Validation in chronic stroke and across independent samples is further required.

papers.title: TGAN-TSR: A type-aware graph attention time-spectral representation for heterogeneous fusion networks in gear system fault diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Rotating machinery often demonstrates complex dynamic behaviors, such as nonstationarity, multicycle coupling, and nonlinear coherent frequency components, under different operating conditions. Nevertheless, most existing fault diagnosis methods overlook the intrinsic correlations between heterogeneous features, resulting in incomplete information representation and the loss of critical fault signatures. These limitations impede their application in high-precision fault diagnosis tasks. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Type-aware Graph Attention Network integrating Temporal and Spectral Representations (TGAN-TSR), which incorporates feature-level fusion to enhance feature modeling and discriminative capabilities for rotating machinery fault diagnosis. Advanced signal processing techniques are initially used to extract dominant frequency band components. Together with higher-order spectral analysis, frequency coupling relationships are revealed to construct time-frequency representations that capture the intrinsic characteristics of vibration signals. Subsequently, a dual-channel feature extraction framework is developed to learn deep discriminative features from both temporal and spectral domains, thus enhancing the representation of critical fault patterns. Finally, a type-aware fusion mechanism is introduced, which, combined with a graph-based modeling strategy, facilitates associative learning and hierarchical fusion of multi domain features. Extensive experiments conducted on both public benchmark datasets and a proprietary gearbox dataset demonstrate that the proposed TGAN-TSR effectively captures important fault features and significantly improves diagnostic accuracy. This method provides a reliable and interpretable diagnostic framework for the intelligent operation and maintenance of complex rotating machinery systems.

papers.title: What's in a Story? Studying Neural Narrative Engagement with Auditory Passages Using EEG Inter-Subject Correlation
papers.abstract: Narrative engagement - a state implicating attention as well as emotional and sequential processing - is crucial in contexts ranging from social interaction to education. Yet we still lack an understanding of how narrative contents and listener perceptions relate to the neural responses they elicit. In this study, we investigate relationships between auditory narratives and listener responses using electroencephalography inter-subject correlation (EEG-ISC), a measure of neural synchrony that has been shown to correlate with narrative cohesion, attention, preference, and learning. We analyzed dense-array EEG recorded from 46 adult participants who listened to social and non-social narrated literary excerpts. The data were spatially optimized using Reliable Components Analysis, and ISC was calculated for each of the three maximally reliable components (RCs) on a per-stimulus basis. While we found no significant relationships between EEG-ISC and broad social/non-social categorizations of the excerpts, ISC for high sociocognitive word usage significantly exceeded that of medium and low word usage in the third spatial component, RC3. We further observed a significant positive correlation between participants' summed ratings of interest, compulsion, and enjoyment and ISC, both for RC2 and when summed across RC1-RC3. Interaction analyses suggest that passage content and behavioral responses contributed independently as additive effects to these relationships. Taken together, these findings extend previous research utilizing EEG-ISC in natural speech contexts and, importantly, suggest that the decomposition of EEG into maximally correlated spatial components can separate co-occurring neural processes engaged during story listening.

papers.title: Group-specific associations among sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and frontal alpha asymmetry in college students: evidence from a cross-sectional EEG study.
papers.abstract: Poor sleep quality is associated with depressive symptoms, but its accompanying neurophysiological correlates remain unclear in non-clinical college students. This study examined associations among sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) in students with and without elevated depressive symptoms. This cross-sectional study included 120 college students, comprising 60 students with depressive symptoms (DS) and 60 non-depressed controls (NC), classified using the Self-Rating Depression Scale. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and FAA was derived from resting-state EEG. Analyses included BMI-adjusted group comparisons, partial correlations, regression models, and an exploratory indirect-path analysis. False discovery rate correction was applied to multiple comparisons. After BMI adjustment, the DS group had higher PSQI scores [median (P25, P75): 7 (6, 10) vs. 3 (1, 5)] and lower composite FAA values [-0.041 (-0.116, 0.031) vs. 0.056 (0.017, 0.103); both p < 0.001] than the NC group. Similar FAA differences were observed using frontopolar and frontal electrode-pair indices. PSQI scores were positively correlated with depressive symptoms in both groups (DS: r = 0.412, q = 0.006; NC: r = 0.462, q = 0.001). In the DS group, composite FAA was negatively correlated with PSQI (r = -0.322, q = 0.034) and depressive symptoms (r = -0.388, q = 0.010); neither FAA-related association reached statistical significance in the NC group. After BMI adjustment, PSQI and FAA were jointly associated with depressive symptom severity in the DS group (R 2 = 0.243). An exploratory indirect-path analysis yielded an indirect association estimate of 0.092 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.002-0.202). Poorer sleep quality was associated with greater depressive symptom severity in both groups, whereas FAA-related associations were observed mainly in the DS group. These findings suggest that FAA may be a candidate neurophysiological correlate of the concurrent association between sleep quality and depressive symptoms in non-clinical college students. Causal mediation cannot be inferred from this cross-sectional study.

papers.title: Evaluation of Antiseizure Potential of Rufinamide and Celecoxib Combination in a PTZ-Kindled Mouse Model Through Electrophysiological, Neurobehavioral, and Molecular Analyses.
papers.abstract: Pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced kindling is a well-established experimental model for investigating epileptogenesis and evaluating the therapeutic potential of antiseizure drugs and their novel combinations. The current study investigated whether rufinamide (RUF) and celecoxib (CEL) administered individually and in combination during PTZ-kindling acquisition, attenuate seizure progression and associated neurobehavioral, biochemical, histopathological, and molecular alterations in PTZ-kindled mice. Male mice received 11 injections of PTZ at the dose of 40 mg/kg on alternate days along with daily treatment of RUF, CEL, or RUF + CEL throughout the 21-day kindling protocol. Seizure severity was monitored using behavioral seizure scoring and validated by electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings of cortical epileptiform activity. The results demonstrated that RUF alone and RUF + CEL combination versus PTZ-kindled mice significantly attenuated seizure progression and reduced epileptiform EEG discharges (p < 0.01). Behavioral assessments revealed that treated animals exhibited reduced anxiety-like behavior along with improved cognitive performance (p < 0.05-0.001). In addition, depression-like behavior evaluated by the sucrose preference test was significantly improved (p < 0.01). Biochemical analyses indicated reduced lipid peroxidation (MDA) and enhanced antioxidant defenses including SOD, GPx, and CAT, with normalization of AChE activity (p < 0.05). Furthermore, RUF and CEL treatment significantly downregulated the expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, and GFAP, indicating attenuation of neuroinflammatory responses. Histopathological outcomes further supported these findings, demonstrating preservation of neuronal architecture and increased neuronal persistence in the hippocampal subregions. Collectively, these findings suggest that the RUF + CEL combination provides enhanced protection against PTZ-induced epileptogenesis and its associated neurobehavioral and neuropathological alterations, potentially through complementary modulation of neuronal excitability, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammatory pathways.

papers.title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain.
papers.abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Sublinear responses, consistent with saturation, occurred proximal to stimulation sites, while supralinear responses arose in network-connected sites during the response's late component. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

papers.title: A high-throughput all-optical platform for mapping gene perturbations to electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Electrical phenotyping remains a bottleneck in linking genes to cellular function. We developed a high-throughput all-optical electrophysiology platform combining an engineered human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) line, wide-field voltage imaging, and automated analysis. The hiPSC line integrates inducible NGN2, CRISPR interference, and degron-gated expression of Voltron2 and CheRiff, enabling neuronal differentiation, targeted gene knockdown, and optical electrophysiology. The microscope records approximately 1,500 spiking glutamatergic neurons at 800 Hz across a 4x4 mm field, with larger fields supporting approximately 3,000 neurons at 660 Hz. Automated analysis extracts single-cell voltage traces and quantifies firing patterns, action-potential waveforms, and subthreshold dynamics. Arrayed knockdown of five sodium- and potassium-channel genes produced distinct electrophysiological phenotypes. The engineered hiPSC line also supported optical electrophysiology recordings from motor neurons, astrocytes, and cardiomyocytes. These results establish a scalable platform for high-throughput electrophysiological phenotyping and functional genomics in hiPSC-derived cells.

papers.title: Frontal Low-Frequency Electroencephalographic Coherence in Bipolar Disorder: A Covariate-Controlled Secondary Analysis of a Public Resting-State EEG Feature Dataset.
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo test whether bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with predefined frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp electroencephalography (EEG) coherence differences relative to healthy controls (HC), depressive disorder (DD), and schizophrenia (SZ) in a covariate-controlled reanalysis of a public resting-state EEG feature dataset.MethodsThe covariate-complete sample included 472 participants (93 HC, 66 BD, 196 DD, and 117 SZ). Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) models adjusted for age, sex, education, and intelligence quotient (IQ). Primary outcomes were predefined frontal/frontopolar delta, theta, and combined delta-theta coherence means. Electrode-pair, regional, all-frequency, distributional, global-reference, frontopolar, and age sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.ResultsBD had higher adjusted coherence than all comparison groups across the three primary measures (partial η2 = .037-.040); Holm-adjusted BD-HC, BD-DD, and BD-SZ contrasts were significant for each measure. Features surviving false discovery rate correction were concentrated in the delta and theta bands. Findings were robust to distributional, outlier, and global-coherence analyses, but effects were strongest in frontopolar pairs and attenuated as anterior electrodes were excluded.ConclusionsBD showed higher covariate-adjusted frontal/frontopolar low-frequency scalp coherence than HC within this dataset. Differences from DD and SZ were smaller and concentrated in frontopolar pairs susceptible to ocular artifacts. Because only scalp-level coherence features were available and participant-level artifact-rejection data were unavailable, the findings do not establish a diagnostic biomarker, diagnostic specificity, or source-level mechanism. Artifact-controlled replication is required.

papers.title: Aesthetic preference for the visual appearance of modern decorative cabinets in young adults: An ERP study.
papers.abstract: This study investigated the neural processing underlying aesthetic preferences for the visual appearance of modern decorative cabinets and examined whether cabinets associated with different preference levels elicited distinct event-related potential (ERP) responses. Electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded from 31 young adults while they viewed modern decorative cabinet images and standardized affective pictures from the Chinese Affective Picture System (CAPS), which served as an affective reference set. Participants rated each image using a 5-point scale. Ratings were recoded into three preference levels for behavioral and ERP analyses. Within-participant consistency and between-participant agreement were assessed using repeated cabinet ratings. Repeated cabinet preference ratings were relatively consistent within participants, whereas agreement between participants was limited. In the frontal region, medium-preference cabinet images elicited significantly larger N100 amplitudes than high- and low-preference images. Late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes did not differ significantly across cabinet preference levels, whereas CAPS images showed significant LPP differences across preference levels. Response times were longer for cabinet images than for CAPS images. papers.title: Clinical outcomes and EEG monitoring in absence epilepsy trials: A narrative review.
papers.abstract: Absence epilepsy is characterized by typical absence seizures with distinct electroclinical signatures. The main semiological feature is sudden behavioral arrest associated with brief impairment of consciousness, and the electroencephalographic (EEG) hallmark pattern is generalized, symmetric 2.5-4 Hz spike-and-wave discharges (GSW). Absence epilepsy diagnosis relies on correlating GSW with observable clinical manifestations. Monitoring therapeutic effects based solely on reported symptoms may be misleading, as behavioral arrest can be difficult to identify. Patients often do not recall most seizures, and observable motor/behavioral signs may be subtle, such as minimal twitches or transient lapses in responsiveness, which may go unnoticed. In clinical trials for absence epilepsies, quantification of GSW activity by EEG offers an objective and accurate measure of electrical burden and therapeutic efficacy. Despite technological limitations, GSW remains a robust neurophysiological endpoint. Increasing evidence indicates that the timing and burden of GSW correlate with epilepsy comorbidities, including attention, cognition, behavior, and sleep. We reviewed the published literature regarding GSW as an outcome measure in absence epilepsy, including nonseizure outcomes and comorbidities. Our review highlights (1) nearly 100% of clinical absence seizures exhibit sustained GSW discharges on EEG; (2) >49% of electrographic seizures are asymptomatic, indicating that reliance on seizure diaries without EEG monitoring underestimates seizure frequency and burden; (3) Genetic Generalized Epilepsy is not a benign condition and is associated with a high prevalence of cognitive and behavioral comorbidities, supporting evaluation beyond clinically observable seizures and the use of prolonged (≥24-h) EEG monitoring; (4) circadian and multidien cycles further emphasize the need for prolonged EEG recordings to reduce timing-related bias; and (5) antiseizure medications effective in absence epilepsy reduce GSW, supporting EEG monitoring as an objective treatment outcome measure. We therefore recommend incorporating ≥24-h EEG in future clinical trials, especially in (young) adults, and exploring comorbidities as important outcome measures. PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: Absence epilepsy causes brief episodes in which a person suddenly stops what they are doing and may not be aware of their surroundings. Many of these seizures have no obvious signs and are often missed or forgotten, meaning seizure diaries alone do not show the full picture. Our review shows that brain recordings (electroencephalographic, EEG), especially when done over 24 h or longer, detect many unrecognized seizures and better measure how well treatments work. EEG findings are also linked to problems with attention, thinking, behavior, and sleep, highlighting the need to look beyond visible seizures when evaluating treatments in clinical trials.

papers.title: Depressive symptoms moderate daily anticipated and momentary emotion dynamics and associate with complex brain network topology: Resting-state EEG and ecological momentary assessment evidence.
papers.abstract: The dynamic linkage between anticipated and momentary emotion is a core daily regulatory process, yet the psychopathological and neurophysiological mechanisms disrupting this linkage in depression remain unclear. By bridging macroscopic neural topology with microscopic behavioral dynamics, this study investigated the within-person dynamics of these emotions and their cross-level associations with depressive symptoms and brain network topology. Integrating resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) with a 14-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA; 3 assessments/day), we recruited 96 young adults. Minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis was applied to characterize baseline brain network topology across multiple frequency bands. Dynamic structural equation modeling (DSEM) was employed to examine within-person dynamics and cross-level statistical moderation. Anticipated emotion prospectively predicted subsequent momentary positive emotion (β = .191) and inversely predicted momentary negative emotion (β = -.125). However, baseline depressive symptoms significantly moderated this prospective affective dynamic: Johnson-Neyman analyses identified empirical transition ranges (PHQ-9 scores 5.7-9.7; mild symptom range) beyond which the prospective emotional link attenuated to non-significance. Furthermore, topological metrics in the theta and delta bands exhibited indirect statistical associations with daily emotional dynamics via their cross-sectional relationship with baseline depressive symptoms. An attenuated prospective association between positive anticipation and subsequent momentary emotional experience represents a key affective alteration in depressive distress. This daily emotional attenuation co-occurs with elevated depressive distress and is indirectly associated with a centralized topological organization in low-frequency resting-state brain networks. These findings provide novel neurophysiological indicators and highlight the critical window for ecological interventions before symptom severity reaches the moderate range.

papers.title: Rituximab-responsive epilepsia partialis continua in autoimmune Polyendocrine syndrome: A video-EEG-EMG polygraphic study.
papers.abstract: Epilepsia partialis continua (EPC) is a rare and challenging form of focal motor status epilepticus. Its occurrence strictly in systemic autoimmune disorders without overt encephalitis is exceptional. Corticosteroids are first-line therapy but may be limited by significant side effects and poor metabolic tolerability. We report a 54-year-old woman with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome (APS), including autoimmune hepatitis, latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, celiac disease, and hypothyroidism, presenting with continuous jerks of right III-V fingers. Neurological examination showed continuous, irregular jerks confined to the right III, IV, and V fingers. Extensive serum and CSF screenings, including neuronal antibodies, and MRI were unremarkable. Ictal HMPAO-SPECT revealed a focal hyperperfusion in the left hand-knob area of the primary motor cortex. Brain FDG-PET revealed focal hypometabolism in the same region. Video-EEG-EMG polygraphy showed intermittent spikes and polyspikes over the left central region preceding EMG bursts of the right V finger's abductor muscle with a latency of approximately 30-40 ms. These findings were consistent with EPC. Corticosteroids induced marked improvement but were discontinued due to severe glycemic worsening. Subsequent treatment with oral steroids, IVIG, and multiple antiseizure medications were ineffective. Administration of Rituximab led to complete and sustained clinical and electrophysiological remission, which persisted at the 18-month follow-up. EPC can be a severe, focal manifestation of systemic autoimmunity even without encephalitis. Rituximab represents an effective steroid-sparing option for refractory autoimmune EPC, particularly in metabolically vulnerable patients.

papers.title: Nonverbal reasoning in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy: associations with gross motor function, MRI, and EEG findings.
papers.abstract: To examine the association between gross motor function level and Raven's Colored Progressive Matrices (CPM) performance in children and adolescents with cerebral palsy (CP), compare CPM performance with typically developing participants, and explore associations with MRI and EEG findings. This multicenter cross-sectional study included 40 participants with CP and 20 comparison participants aged 10-17 years. CPM totals were converted to center-derived age-referenced scores; the upper available normative age band was applied above age 11.5 years. Gross motor function was classified with the GMFCS. Clinically indicated MRI and EEG findings were categorized using prespecified systems. Median CPM score was 72 (IQR 64-81) in the CP group and 98 (IQR 92-104) in the comparison group (adjusted difference -26.4, 95% CI -31.2 to -21.6). GMFCS level was inversely associated with CPM score (Spearman rho = -.78, 95% CI -.85 to -.68). Predominant white matter injury was associated with lower CPM scores. The adjusted association with epileptiform EEG abnormalities was inconclusive. CPM performance was associated with GMFCS level and MRI pattern, but the cross-sectional findings do not establish causality. Gross motor classification must not substitute for accessible neuropsychological assessment.

papers.title: Safety, Signal Quality, and Patient Satisfaction With Insertable Loop Recorder Implantation by Specialized Electrophysiology Nurses: Prospective Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Insertable loop recorders (ILRs) are subcutaneous cardiac monitoring devices used in the diagnosis of arrhythmias and in the etiological investigation of syncope and cryptogenic stroke. Device miniaturization and procedural simplification have facilitated implantation in ambulatory settings. The involvement of specialized electrophysiology nurses may help meet rising clinical demand, although evidence in our setting remains limited. This study aimed to analyze implantation safety, detection signal quality, adverse events during follow-up, and patient satisfaction when the procedure was performed by specialized nurses. This prospective observational study (the CARDIONURSE study) was conducted in the Arrhythmia Unit of Hospital General Universitario Doctor Balmis between February 2022 and May 2023. Thirty-five patients with a clinical indication for ILR implantation were included. The procedure was performed by 2 specialized nurses under medical supervision. Sociodemographic, clinical, and technical implantation variables were collected, including detection signal amplitude (mV), together with adverse events and follow-up outcomes at 1 and 6 months. Patient satisfaction was assessed using a study-specific questionnaire at 4 time points. Descriptive statistical analysis was performed. Mean age was 71.1 (SD 11.3) years, and 62.9% (22/35) were women. The most frequent indication was syncope (27/35, 77.1%), followed by suspected atrial fibrillation (AF) in cryptogenic stroke (6/35, 17.1%). No objective procedural complications occurred (35/35, 100% of procedures); mild, transient procedural pain was reported in 5.7% (2/35) of patients, and the procedure lasted less than 5 minutes in 74.3% (26/35) of procedures. Mean signal amplitude was 0.45 (SD 0.29) mV, with a visible P wave in 94.3% (33/35) of patients. No wound-related adverse events were recorded among the 85.7% (30/35) of patients with available follow-up data at 6 months; data were unavailable for the remaining 5 patients. A diagnosis was obtained in 20% (6/30) of patients with an available diagnostic outcome at 6 months. Overall, 97.1% (34/35) of patients reported maximum or very high satisfaction with the intervention, and 100% (35/35) with the care received. ILR implantation by specialized electrophysiology nurses in an ambulatory setting is a safe, fast, and technically adequate procedure, with adequate signal quality and high patient satisfaction. These findings support the feasibility of specialized nursing as ILR implanters in similar ambulatory care settings, although confirmation in larger, multicenter studies is warranted before broader implementation.

papers.title: Multimodal characterization of putative pan -inhibitory viral constructs in macaque monkeys.
papers.abstract: Transgenic approaches and validated viral vector toolboxes have advanced our understanding of how inhibitory neurons shape cognition and motor control in mice and other rodents. However, such advances have been elusive in non-human primates (NHPs). While many studies demonstrate expression of reporter proteins, few studies have provided clear quantitative evidence of whether these viral constructs can be reliably used for assessment of in vivo and in vitro function in primates, which, in turn, has hindered widespread adoption by NHP researchers. Here, we characterize putative pan-inhibitory cell targeting vectors engineered with regions from the Dlx5-6 intergenic domain. Pan-inhibitory viral vectors are attractive because they enable ground-truth optotagging and modulation of multiple inhibitory subtypes in the same animal and, when combined with machine learning approaches, enable cell-type classifiers for NHPs. We combined in vivo anesthetized electrophysiological recordings, in vitro slice electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry across seven rhesus macaque monkeys to assess the specificity, completeness and efficacy of three constructs in multiple sensory and higher-order association cortices. The vectors reliably restricted transgene expression to inhibitory neurons (81-97%). However, of the local GABAergic neurons only 32-64% expressed the transgene, depending on the construct. This incompleteness arose in part from uneven coverage across subtypes, with strong transgene expression in parvalbumin-positive interneurons (∼60-90%), sparse expression in calbindin-positive interneurons (∼1-7%), and near-complete avoidance of calretinin-positive interneurons. A construct pairing DLX2.0 with ChrimsonR was excellent for in vivo optotagging, while h56D paired with bReaChES most effectively suppressed neural activity in vivo . In the slice, activating terminals of transgene-expressing neurons optically evoked inhibitory currents in coupled pyramidal neurons confirming transsynaptic functionality of these constructs and their use for inhibitory circuit-specific synaptic assessments and manipulation. Collectively, the results provide rigorous functional characterization, and quantitative guidance for NHP researchers seeking to deploy GABAergic cell-type-specific tools in their experiments.

papers.title: Human herpesvirus 7-associated encephalitis diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing in pediatric patients: a retrospective study.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to describe the clinical features, treatment and prognosis of immunocompetent children with human herpes virus 7 (HHV-7)-associated encephalitis. Sixteen children with HHV-7-associated encephalitis were diagnosed by metagenomic next-generation sequencing of their cerebrospinal fluid and followed up for 3 months. The median age of the cohort was 8.6 years (range, 1.4-11.8) and comprised of 8 males and 8 females. The most common presenting symptoms were fever (12/16, 75.0%), headache (10/16, 62.5%), and vomiting (8/16, 50.0%). Abnormal electroencephalography and encephalitis-related neuroimaging findings were obtained in 50.0% (6/12) and 25.0% (4/16) of the patients, respectively. 68.8% of the patients were treated with either acyclovir or ganciclovir. Unfavorable outcomes occurred in three patients, including the death of a 2-year-old child. Pediatric HHV-7-associated encephalitis generally has a favorable prognosis, but severe cases do occur. Early recognition is important for increasing clinicians' awareness of this condition.
